questions.title: How does GRPO compute advantages without a critic, and how is credit assigned across tokens?
questions.question_body: In the paper, PPO uses a value function and GAE to compute token-level advantages. GRPO instead sets per-token advantages from group-normalized rewards: for outcome supervision, \(\hat{A}_{i,t} = \tilde r_i = (r_i - \mathrm{mean}(\mathbf{r}))/\mathrm{std}(\mathbf{r})\) for all \(t\) in an output \(o_i\), and for process supervision, \(\hat{A}_{i,t} = \sum_{\mathrm{index}(j) \ge t} \tilde r_i^{\mathrm{index}(j)}\). Without a learned value baseline or discounting, how does GRPO handle credit assignment in long chains-of-thought? Does dividing by \(|o_i|\) fully mitigate length bias, and did you observe instability for very long outputs?

questions.title: What exactly is the per-token KL regularization in GRPO, and why is the estimator called unbiased and positive?
questions.question_body: GRPO adds a KL penalty between the trained policy and a reference policy directly in the loss using the estimator \(\mathbb{D}_{KL}[\pi_{\theta} \Vert \pi_{ref}] = \frac{\pi_{ref}(o_{i,t}\mid q,o_{i,<t})}{\pi_{\theta}(o_{i,t}\mid q,o_{i,<t})} - \log\frac{\pi_{ref}(o_{i,t}\mid q,o_{i,<t})}{\pi_{\theta}(o_{i,t}\mid q,o_{i,<t})} - 1\). Under which expectation is this estimator unbiased (e.g., \(\mathbb{E}_{o_{i,t}\sim \pi_{\theta}}\))? How is it aggregated across tokens and samples? The expression is always nonnegative because \(x - \log x - 1 \ge 0\) for \(x>0\), but could you clarify in what precise sense it is unbiased for the true KL?

questions.title: Are GRPO’s loss-level KL penalties equivalent to PPO’s reward-level KL penalties in expectation?
questions.question_body: PPO typically incorporates per-token KL via a penalty in the reward, e.g., \(r_t = r_\varphi(q,o_{\le t}) - \beta \log \frac{\pi_{\theta}(o_t\mid q,o_{<t})}{\pi_{ref}(o_t\mid q,o_{<t})}\). GRPO instead adds \(\beta\, \mathbb{D}_{KL}[\pi_{\theta} \Vert \pi_{ref}]\) directly to the loss. Are these two regularizations equivalent (up to constants) under the clipped objective and sequence-level averaging, or do they lead to systematically different gradient directions? Any empirical observations on stability vs. controllability of KL with GRPO?

questions.title: Does z-scoring rewards within each group bias GRPO toward relative rather than absolute quality?
questions.question_body: For a question \(q\), GRPO samples \(G\) outputs, scores them, and uses group-normalized rewards \(\tilde r_i = (r_i - \mathrm{mean}(\mathbf{r}))/\mathrm{std}(\mathbf{r})\). In standard policy gradient, subtracting a baseline preserves unbiasedness, but dividing by a batch-dependent \(\mathrm{std}(\mathbf{r})\) changes the effective step size and relative scaling. Does this normalization change the optimal policy or only rescale gradients? How sensitive are results to \(G\) and to the variance of \(r_i\)?

questions.title: How are process rewards normalized when outputs have different numbers of steps, and does this overweight longer solutions?
questions.question_body: For process supervision, you collect step-end rewards across the group, \(\mathbf{R} = \{r_i^{\mathrm{index}(j)}\}\), then normalize using the mean and standard deviation over all step rewards across all \(G\) outputs. Since longer outputs contribute more step-end points, does this bias the normalization toward longer chains-of-thought? Did you try per-output normalization or weighting schemes to avoid overweighting longer samples?

questions.title: What happens if the group reward standard deviation is zero during normalization?
questions.question_body: If all \(G\) outputs for a question receive nearly identical rewards (e.g., all wrong with rule-based rewards), then \(\mathrm{std}(\mathbf{r}) \approx 0\). How do you handle this numerically in GRPO (e.g., adding \(\epsilon\), skipping the update, or falling back to a default advantage)?

questions.title: How exactly are the \(G\) samples per question generated in GRPO, and how sensitive is performance to decoding settings?
questions.question_body: You mention using naive nucleus sampling during exploration. What specific decoding parameters did you use for GRPO sampling (temperature, top-p, max length, frequency/presence penalties)? Did you study sensitivity to these choices or compare against beam search or tree-search decoders?

questions.title: Algorithm 1 vs. training details: is there one GRPO update per exploration batch or multiple?
questions.question_body: Algorithm 1 shows an inner loop with GRPO updates repeated \(\mu\) times per batch, but the training details later say the policy model only has a single update following each exploration stage. Should I interpret this run as \(\mu = 1\), or are these describing different experiments?

questions.title: How is the reference model updated in GRPO, and does frequently setting \(\pi_{ref} \leftarrow \pi_{\theta}\) weaken KL control?
questions.question_body: The algorithm sets \(\pi_{ref}\) to the current \(\pi_{\theta}\) at each outer iteration. This seems to keep the KL penalty small because the reference keeps chasing the policy. How often do you refresh \(\pi_{ref}\) in practice, and did you compare to a fixed SFT reference? How do you ensure sufficient regularization against drift or verbosity?

questions.title: With \(G=64\) samples per question, is GRPO actually more compute-efficient than PPO with a critic?
questions.question_body: You argue GRPO reduces memory by removing the critic, but GRPO requires sampling \(G=64\) outputs per question and scoring them. In practice (for a 7B policy), how do wall-clock time, GPU memory, and tokens processed per second compare between GRPO (no critic, many samples) and PPO (critic of similar size, fewer samples)?

questions.title: How are reasoning step boundaries detected for process supervision to compute \(\mathrm{index}(j)\)?
questions.question_body: Process rewards rely on step-end token indices \(\mathrm{index}(j)\) within chain-of-thought text. How are steps detected and token-aligned in free-form CoT? Are steps explicitly annotated with special tags, identified by regex rules (e.g., lines starting with "Step"), or predicted by a separate model? How robust is this across English and Chinese?

questions.title: Why is there no discount factor in process-supervised advantages, and did you try discounted returns?
questions.question_body: The process advantage is defined as \(\hat{A}_{i,t} = \sum_{\mathrm{index}(j) \ge t} \tilde r_i^{\mathrm{index}(j)}\), without a discount \(\gamma\). Did you experiment with discounted returns to reduce variance or to de-emphasize distant steps, especially for very long chains-of-thought? If so, what was the effect?

questions.title: Why does RL improve Maj@K but not Pass@K, and how exactly are these two metrics computed here?
questions.question_body: You report that RL improves Maj@K but not Pass@K and hypothesize it makes the output distribution more robust rather than increasing fundamental capability. Could you provide your precise definitions and settings (values of \(K\), decoding parameters) and an interpretation: does RL increase the mode probability of correct solutions while reducing the diversity of correct-but-rare solutions?

questions.title: How is benchmark decontamination applied to Chinese and chain-of-thought text with the 10-gram rule?
questions.question_body: The decontamination removes any text containing an exact 10-gram match to benchmark substrings, or exact matches for shorter substrings (\(\ge 3\)-grams). For languages without whitespace segmentation (e.g., Chinese) and for chain-of-thought rationales, how are n-grams defined (characters, tokens)? How do you mitigate false positives from common phrases vs. false negatives from minor rephrasings?

questions.title: Why use a 10% threshold to flag math-related domains in Common Crawl mining, and what bias might this introduce?
questions.question_body: You label a domain as math-related if over 10% of its pages are recalled by the fastText classifier, then manually annotate math-relevant URLs within that domain. How was the 10% chosen, and did you evaluate the risk of (a) missing sparse math sources or (b) over-including domains where a minority of math pages are highly templated, potentially biasing the corpus?

questions.title: When you keep the top 40B tokens in iteration 1, how is a token-level cutoff derived from page-level scores?
questions.question_body: Pages are ranked by fastText scores, but selection is described in terms of tokens (e.g., top 40B tokens). Do you keep full pages until a token budget is reached, truncate long pages, or weight by score? Are there per-domain or per-host caps to prevent a few sites from dominating the early iterations?

questions.title: The paper says 40B HTML web pages after deduplication—can you clarify whether this is pages or tokens?
questions.question_body: The data collection section mentions reducing Common Crawl to 40B HTML web pages via URL and near-duplicate deduplication. That number seems very large for pages. Is this a typo for 40B tokens, or does it refer to unique URLs processed before filtering? Could you detail the dedup procedure and the actual page counts?

questions.title: What explains the lack of gains from arXiv-only training, and did you control for LaTeX tokenization and boilerplate?
questions.question_body: You observe that training on MathPile or ArXiv-RedPajama yields no improvement or even deterioration on GSM8K, MATH, MMLU-STEM, and miniF2F. Could this be due to LaTeX-heavy tokenization, math symbol coverage in the tokenizer, or residual boilerplate (references, macros) hurting signal-to-noise? Did you test smaller arXiv mixtures or specialized tokenizers?

questions.title: How were the 7B pretraining mixture ratios enforced across 500B tokens—fixed sampling or curriculum scheduling?
questions.question_body: For DeepSeekMath-Base 7B, the mix is 56% DeepSeekMath Corpus, 4% AlgebraicStack, 10% arXiv, 20% GitHub code, 10% general CC NL. Were these ratios enforced per-batch throughout training, adjusted over time (e.g., curriculum), or temperature-sampled? How did you prevent catastrophic forgetting of coding while maximizing math gains?

questions.title: Program-of-thought evaluation: what execution environment, libraries, and answer checking criteria were used?
questions.question_body: For PoT, models write Python using libraries like math and sympy. What sandbox was used (timeout, memory, disabled IO/network), which libraries and versions were allowed, and how were answers compared (exact string, numeric tolerance, rational simplification)? Any safeguards against non-determinism affecting scores?

questions.title: How does dividing the GRPO objective by sequence length interact with length bias and group normalization?
questions.question_body: The GRPO loss averages per token, i.e., multiplies clipped ratios by \(\hat{A}_{i,t}\) and averages over \(t=1..|o_i|\). With outcome supervision where \(\hat{A}_{i,t}=\tilde r_i\) for all tokens, this seems to make the total update magnitude per sample roughly proportional to \(\tilde r_i\), independent of \(|o_i|\). Does this eliminate incentives for verbosity or terseness, or did you still observe length-related failure modes?

questions.title: What prevents degenerate behaviors (verbosity, hedging, premature EoS) when only final outcomes are rewarded?
questions.question_body: Under outcome supervision, the only reward is at the end of the output. Besides the KL term, do you include any format or extraction rewards to encourage concise, well-structured rationales? Did process supervision measurably reduce verbosity or improve intermediate step correctness compared to outcome-only GRPO?
